My recommendations if you're struggling to increase vitamin D levels despite supplementation:

Make sure you're getting enough magnesium. It's an essential cofactor for vitamin D metabolism. I recommend ~300–400 mg daily from diet and supplements. Magnesium glycinate is a good supplemental form.

Choose a reputable, third-party-tested vitamin D3 supplement. Studies have found large discrepancies between the amount of vitamin D on the label and what's actually in the product.

Consider a more bioavailable form of vitamin D3 if you're struggling to increase your levels (VESIsorb is one formulation I mentioned to Tim).

There's no one-size-fits-all dose! Genetics, absorption, and individual metabolism all affect how much vitamin D you need.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick on why your vitamin D might not come up even when you take it.

1. Get enough magnesium. It helps the body use vitamin D. She suggests about 300 to 400 mg a day from food and supplements.
2. Buy a third-party-tested D3. Studies found big gaps between the label and what's in the bottle.
3. Some people absorb it better in other forms.
4. There's no one dose for everyone.

Get a blood test before you guess. Then test again.

hits.text:
Did you know visceral fat shrinks more readily than the fat under your skin?

Visceral fat, the fat packed around the organs deep in the abdomen, responds to stress hormones very differently than subcutaneous fat.

Adrenaline and noradrenaline (the catecholamines) tell fat cells to release stored fat. Fat cells "hear" these hormones through two kinds of receptors. Beta receptors push fat release forward. Alpha-2 receptors put the brakes on.

Human studies comparing fat taken from inside the abdomen with fat from under the skin show a consistent pattern. Visceral fat cells carry more of the "go" signal and less of the "brake." When catecholamines rise, visceral fat releases its stored fat more readily.

Visceral fat also listens less to insulin. Normally, insulin holds fat inside fat cells. In visceral fat, that hold is weaker. This is part of why excess visceral fat is so metabolically harmful, since it spills fat straight toward the liver. It also means visceral fat is primed to be mobilized.

Exercise is one of the most reliable ways to raise catecholamines. Adrenaline and noradrenaline climb with physical effort. In controlled trials, exercise reduces visceral fat, and pooled analyses show this happens even when overall weight loss is modest. Exercise appears to preferentially target the deep abdominal fat.

Cold exposure raises them too. Immersing in cold water sharply raises noradrenaline in humans, and visceral fat is especially sensitive to noradrenaline. It's reasonable to expect that regular cold exposure would help draw down visceral fat, much like exercise does.

Keeping insulin low matters too. Because insulin opposes fat release, frequent spikes work against the signal catecholamines send. Pairing movement or cold with lower insulin, by limiting refined carbohydrates and frequent snacking, makes it easier for visceral fat to release what it stores.

If someone wants to reduce the fat that does the most metabolic damage, it's clear that regular exercise is a reliable tool, that cold exposure is a sensible addition, and that keeping insulin in check helps both work better.

Is this why our food is making us sick? 

In 1958, Congress created a narrow exemption so everyday ingredients like salt, vinegar, and baking soda could skip the full formal review process required for new food additives. The idea was simple: if something had a long history of safe use and was generally recognized as safe by experts, it did not need the same premarket scrutiny. Decades later, that modest exception has become the main route for most new substances entering the American food supply.

Under the modern GRAS system, a company can decide on its own that a chemical or novel ingredient is safe. It is not required to notify the FDA, let alone wait for approval. Even when a company does submit a voluntary notice, it can withdraw the filing if the agency raises questions and still put the ingredient on the market. Estimates suggest hundreds of substances have entered foods this way with little or no independent review. Analyses show that roughly 99 percent of new food chemicals introduced since 2000 used the GRAS pathway rather than the formal additive petition process. 

Safety assessments are frequently conducted by people with clear financial ties to the manufacturer—company employees, paid consultants, or expert panels selected by the company itself. Studies of hundreds of GRAS notices have found conflicts of interest nearly ubiquitous. A small circle of recurring experts has dominated many of these panels for years. The FDA has issued guidance intended to reduce bias, yet independent analyses indicate it is often ignored. 

The practical result is limited transparency. The agency lacks a complete public inventory of every self-affirmed GRAS substance, the amounts used, or the specific foods involved. Cumulative exposure from multiple related chemicals is rarely evaluated. When problems surface later, post-market action has historically been slow. 

A former senior FDA official once acknowledged that the agency simply does not have the information needed to vouch for the safety of many of these substances.
This is not a technical quirk. It is a structural shift that places primary responsibility for determining what is safe in the hands of the companies that profit from the ingredients. 

Consumers and independent researchers are left with incomplete data about what is actually in the food supply and why it was allowed there. For substances with centuries of ordinary culinary use, the original intent of the law still makes sense. For the steady stream of newer chemicals entering through the same door, the shortcomings are harder to ignore.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Many people believe the brain needs a steady supply of dietary carbohydrate or it will stop working. The brain can run on more than glucose.

In 1967, Owen and colleagues studied a small group of people who fasted for several weeks and measured what the brain was using for fuel. Ketones had replaced glucose as the brain's main energy source.

When carbohydrate intake is low and insulin falls, the body starts pulling on stored fat. The liver turns that fat into ketones, which travel through the blood to the brain, where brain cells readily take them up and burn them for energy. This is a normal, built-in part of human metabolism.

It also helps to separate two things that often get lumped together. Dietary carbohydrate and blood glucose are different. The liver and kidneys make glucose on their own, so the body keeps glucose in the blood even when someone eats no carbohydrate at all.

That leaves an interesting question. Could brain tissue keep working if glucose were taken away completely and ketones were the only fuel on offer?

In a paper I recently published with my BYU colleagues, we tested this in mouse brain tissue. We removed glucose from the environment entirely and supplied the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate as the only outside fuel. The mitochondria in the brain tissue kept working. The tissue could also handle and recover from repeated, intense bursts of electrical activity that demand a huge amount of energy. Tissue given no outside fuel at all could not keep up.

This was brain tissue studied in the lab over a short window, and living brains still need more study. Within that setting, ketones powered some of the brain's most energy-hungry work without any outside glucose.

If someone worries that cutting carbs will starve the brain, it's clear that the brain is remarkably flexible about its fuel, and ketones are a fuel it uses very well.

Losing body fat raises your testosterone. Until it starts lowering it.

@drbenhouse describes this as an inverted U. Coming down from a high body fat percentage can move testosterone 50, 100, even 200 points in the right direction. But once body fat starts getting too low, and you keep pushing that caloric deficit, testosterone starts heading back down.

The individual picture is messier than the curve. Population-level data give us a good starting point, but pay attention to individual dynamics. Ben has worked with three clients who lost roughly half of themselves, 300 pounds down to 150, 330 down to 180. One ended up with a testosterone of 850 and was crushing it. One was anemic with testosterone in the tank. One sat around 200. None of the three were under 15 percent body fat.

That's why Ben weighs the relative change more than the absolute number. our brain adapts to your norm, so where you came from matters as much as where you are now.

The population data guides the individual. It does not tell you where your own line sits.

What if a simple metabolic marker in your mid-50s quietly predicted how well your memory would hold up in your mid-70s?

A 20-year Finnish follow-up study (from the Health 2000 cohort, published in Neurobiology of Aging) tracked people from 
midlife (mean age ~55) into late life (~75). 

Researchers measured insulin resistance (via HOMA-IR) early on, then followed with brain PET imaging for beta-amyloid and repeated cognitive testing.

The key result: People with midlife insulin resistance showed roughly twice the decline in episodic memory over the final 5 years compared with those who had better insulin sensitivity. Higher late-life amyloid burden also predicted steeper memory loss, and the midlife insulin-resistance effect was partly mediated through that amyloid 
accumulation. 

In other words, the metabolic signal from decades earlier was linked to the Alzheimer’s-related pathology that later showed up in the brain.

This is one of the longest looks at midlife insulin resistance and later cognition. It reinforces that the metabolic health you protect (or lose) in your 40s and 50s can still shape cognitive trajectories well into later life—not just through diabetes risk, but through pathways that include brain amyloid.

Midlife isn’t just a dress rehearsal. It’s one of the windows where insulin sensitivity still looks modifiable.
Source: Pietilä et al., Neurobiology of Aging (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2026.06.004
